slides.title: Ch. 21: Graphs and Images
slides.sub: Making graphs and manipulating images: Pillow, ImageDraw, the clipboard and Matplotlib

items.body: Every output on these slides was printed by the Python above when the deck was made, and every picture was saved by a program that is run again to check it. Windows, macOS and a real screen were never used: the clipboard program ran on a virtual display, and what could not be run is marked on its slide.

slides.notes: Chapter 20 taught a program to reach a person. Chapter 21 teaches a program to make pictures: edit them with Pillow, draw on them, put them on the clipboard, and draw graphs with Matplotlib. The chapter has 31 listings, 20 figures and 1 table, and ends with 12 practice questions and 3 practice programs, Tile Maker, the photo folder finder and the seating cards. This deck follows the chapter in its own order: colours and coordinates, cropping, pasting, resizing, rotating, pixels, Project 16 that adds a logo to every picture, shapes and text, the clipboard, and graphs with line, scatter, bar and pie. It adds what the research found when every printed output was run again: Table 21-1 gives Green as the colour that CSS calls lime; a PNG saved without a dpi has no pixel density although the chapter says 72; the fill of a rotated corner follows the mode of the image and not the operating system; Appendix A pins matplotlib==3.92, which does not exist; Appendix B answers 3, 6 and 12 wrongly or partly wrongly; the printed listing of Project 16 has an en dash that stops it with a SyntaxError; textsize and getsize exist only in Pillow 9.5.0; and plt.pie returns a tuple up to Matplotlib 3.10.8 and a PieContainer from 3.11. The outputs of this chapter are pictures, so the deck shows real ones: sixteen pictures that programs saved are on the slides as images, and each caption names the program that made the picture. The build runs every such program again and refuses the deck unless the slide holds a picture that is byte for byte, or pixel for pixel, what the program saves now. Every output on the slides was printed by Python 3.14.6, installed with uv, with Pillow 12.3.0, Matplotlib 3.11.2, NumPy 2.5.4 and pyperclipimg 0.2.0. Four programs download the publisher's zip of online materials and check each of the four files of the chapter against its SHA-256. Windows and macOS were never used, and nobody looked at a real screen: the clipboard program ran on a virtual display, which the slide says. What could not be run, Windows and macOS, the windows of Matplotlib and of Image.show on a real screen, and two Matplotlib releases on Python 3.14.6, is marked on its slide.

slides.notes: The route has six parts. It starts with colours, grids and coordinates: what a program can do with one image, the first scanned picture as a grid of numbers, colours and Table 21-1, and the coordinates and box tuples. Then the editing: cropping, pasting and tiling, masks and the alpha channel, resizing, rotating and flipping, and saving as PNG or JPEG with the question of pixel density. The third part is Project 16, a logo on every picture, as a flow chart and as the file that ships. The fourth is drawing shapes, text and fonts, the Pillow releases that changed the chapter, and the practice programs. The fifth is the clipboard and Matplotlib: the four graphs, the pins of Appendix A run now, the life of a pyplot figure and showing a graph in a window. The last part is a one-map summary and the resources. The ranges name the exact slides, so you can return to the part you need. Four of the six stories are on slides, each with a link, and two, on PNG and on JPEG, are told in the notes of the slide about saving; the eight narrative diagrams of the chapter are drawn from the same specifications as the interactive page. Every output was printed by Python 3.14.6 with Pillow 12.3.0, Matplotlib 3.11.2, NumPy 2.5.4 and pyperclipimg 0.2.0, the clipboard ran on a virtual display, and what could not be run is marked on its slide.
slides.take: Six parts, from a grid of numbers to a graph.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: The chapter's own competency questions; the summary comes back to each

items: Which parts of a program that edits pictures, draws on them and plots graphs can be shown to work, and which can only be shown to fail, on a machine that has no screen, no clipboard owner and no Windows or macOS?

Which printed outputs, programs, numbers and statements of the chapter differ in current releases of Python, Pillow and Matplotlib, with the versions its appendix pins, with the operating system of the reader, or in the files and pages it points to, and on what source?

slides.notes: The first question is the spine of the chapter, and the deck answers it slide by slide. On a machine with no screen, a program can make a picture, change it, draw on it, save it and read its pixels back, and the picture can be compared with what was meant; that is what can be shown to work. What can only be shown to fail on such a machine is the part that needs a person's screen: plt.show() and Image.show() open a window, and the clipboard needs a display and a clipboard owner. The research used a virtual X display, Xvfb, with the real xclip, and a Tk window on it, and took a screenshot of the screen; nobody looked at a real monitor, Windows and macOS were never used, and the deck says so where it comes up. The second question is the watch-out. The chapter's 138 interactive statements were replayed as printed in four environments. With Python 3.14.6, Pillow 12.3.0 and Matplotlib 3.11.2, 131 of 138 matched the book headless and 135 on a virtual X display; with the Pillow 10.4.0 and Matplotlib 3.9.2 that Appendix A pins, built from source on 3.14.6, 125 matched headless and 108 on the display; with the same pins as wheels on Python 3.13.14, 129 and 108; with an empty Python, 15. The three that still differ with the newest packages and a display are os.chdir to a Windows path, the font arial.ttf, and the printed tuple of plt.pie, which is a PieContainer. The online materials of the book, 91 files, hold the four files of this chapter and not the others the chapter names. Each slide says where a printed line differs and on what evidence.
slides.take: Know what can be shown to work and what can only be shown to fail.

slides.title: A picture is a grid of numbers
slides.sub: 1957: one of the first scanned photographs was 176 by 176 pixels, one bit each

items: 1957: a drum scanner at the NBS
One bit each: black or white

items.who: Russell A. Kirsch, an engineer whose group at the National Bureau of Standards developed a drum scanner
items.where: The National Bureau of Standards (now NIST), where Kirsch had joined the team that ran the computer SEAC in 1951

slides.notes: Wikipedia's article on Russell A. Kirsch says that in 1957 his group developed a drum scanner, and that one of the first photographs scanned was a picture of his three-month-old son, Walden. It was captured as just 30,976 pixels, a 176 x 176 array, in an area of 5 cm x 5 cm. The bit depth was one bit per pixel, black or white with no shades of gray. In this study Image.new('1', (176, 176)) made a picture of mode 1 with 30,976 pixels, each holding 0 or 1. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Russell A. Kirsch' (the 1957 scan of his three-month-old son Walden; 30,976 pixels, a 176 x 176 array, one bit per pixel), read 2026-10-13; this study's leaves ImageModes and NewImage. The console on the slide uses only Pillow, so each row can be typed into a Python that has Pillow: Image.new('1', (176, 176)) makes a picture of mode 1, one bit for each pixel, size (176, 176), 30,976 pixels; tobytes() packs eight pixels into a byte, so it holds 3,872 bytes, which is 30,976 divided by 8. A new picture is all zero, black; putpixel() writes a 1 and returns None, and getpixel() reads it back, while the pixel beside it is still 0. The same two calls work for the RGB pictures of the rest of the chapter, with a tuple of three integers in place of 0 or 1. The chapter's own first section, Computer Image Fundamentals, says the same thing in words: a picture is a grid of pixels and each pixel is numbers.
slides.take: Every picture you open began as a grid of numbers.

slides.notes: A colour in Pillow is a tuple of four integers from 0 to 255: red, green, blue and alpha. ImageColor.getcolor(name, 'RGBA') turns a colour name or a hex string into that tuple, and the name is not case sensitive: CornflowerBlue gives (100, 149, 237, 255), and #CCDDEE gives (204, 221, 238, 255). The strip of six colours under the program is the picture that the program saved; its caption names the program, and the build runs the program again and compares the picture with this one. The research compared Table 21-1 of the book with Pillow 12.3.0. Of its 8 rows only Green differs: the table says Green is (0, 255, 0, 255), but that is lime in the CSS list that Pillow follows, and the strip shows both side by side, a dark green and a bright one. ImageColor.colormap holds 148 names, from aliceblue to yellowgreen, where the Pillow page says some 140 and the chapter more than 100; and 'transparent' is not one of them, so getcolor() raises ValueError. The new picture of the chapter, Image.new('RGBA', (100, 200), 'purple'), has the pixel (128, 0, 128, 255); with no colour an RGBA picture is the invisible (0, 0, 0, 0). The program was cut from colorsAndModes_v1_0_0.py of the corpus, which also ran: RGBA to JPEG raised OSError with cannot write mode RGBA as JPEG, and an unknown extension raised ValueError.
slides.take: Green of Table 21-1 is lime; Pillow's green is (0, 128, 0).

slides.title: Coordinates and box tuples
slides.sub: The origin is top left; a box keeps its left and top, not its right and bottom

rows: IndexError: image index out of range
items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6; no row reads the clock or the network

items.body: image boxTuple.png made by boxTupleCut_v1_0_0.py

Appendix B, answer 3, calls the box left, top, width and height; the chapter, and Pillow, say left, top, right and bottom. The picture is Figure 21-2 drawn by a program: 6 columns and 5 rows are orange, the box (3, 1, 9, 6) is their size.

slides.notes: A pixel is addressed by (x, y), with the origin at the top left, x growing to the right and y growing down; the last pixel of a 28 by 27 picture is (27, 26), (28, 0) raises IndexError with image index out of range, and a negative x counts from the right edge. A box tuple has four integers in the order left, top, right, bottom, and the box includes the left and top edge and excludes the right and bottom one. The box (3, 1, 9, 6) of Figure 21-2 covers 6 columns and 5 rows, which is 30 pixels; the width is right minus left, not the third number, and a box with right smaller than left raises ValueError with the text Coordinate 'right' is less than 'left'. The picture on the right is made by the program boxTupleCut: it paints the pixels 3 to 8 and 1 to 5 orange on a white 28 by 27 picture, crops the box (3, 1, 9, 6) and finds only orange in it, then crops one column more to the left and finds white; it then enlarges the picture ten times without smoothing and draws a grid so the pixels can be counted. Appendix B of the book answers question 3 by calling a box left, top, width and height, where the chapter says right and bottom; the next slide shows the answer to question 6. Rectangles in ImageDraw are different again: both end points are painted, which the drawing slide counts.
slides.take: Right and bottom are not in the box; the width is right minus left.

items.who: Alvy Ray Smith and Ed Catmull, and later Thomas Porter and Tom Duff
items.where: The New York Institute of Technology Computer Graphics Lab
items.when: The late 1970s, with a paper in 1984

slides.notes: Wikipedia's article on alpha compositing says the concept of an alpha channel was introduced by Alvy Ray Smith and Ed Catmull in the late 1970s at the New York Institute of Technology Computer Graphics Lab. It adds that a 1984 paper by Thomas Porter and Tom Duff introduced premultiplied alpha. The fourth number of an RGBA tuple in chapter 21 is that alpha, from 0 for clear to 255 for solid. In this study a blue square with alpha 128 pasted with itself as the mask over a red one gave the pixel (127, 0, 128). The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Alpha compositing' (alpha channel introduced by Smith and Catmull in the late 1970s; Porter and Duff in 1984), read 2026-10-13; this study's leaves PasteMask and RgbaTuple. The third argument of paste() is a mask, and the program shows what it does with catlogo.png of the book's online materials, which is 100 by 95 pixels in mode LA, a grey channel and an alpha channel, with the corner pixel (255, 0): white and fully clear. Pasted onto a red picture with the logo as its own mask, the corner stays the red (200, 0, 0, 255); pasted without a mask the same corner is copied as (255, 255, 255, 0), so the invisible pixels of the copy overwrite what is below them. That is Figure 21-13 of the book, and the picture on the right shows both results next to each other. The last lines are the story's own experiment: a blue square at alpha 128 pasted over a red pixel with itself as the mask gives (127, 0, 128), half of each. In the corpus program tileMaker_v1_0_0.py, which also ran, pasting the LA logo onto an RGB picture with no mask runs without an error and gives white and black pixels, and with the logo as the mask the transparent corner stays white.
slides.take: Alpha is how much of the top picture you see.

slides.notes: rotate() turns a picture counterclockwise and keeps its size; the corners that no pixel reaches are filled. The chapter says that rotation gaps are black on Windows and transparent on macOS and Linux; on Linux the fill followed the mode of the picture: an RGB picture got (0, 0, 0), an RGBA copy got (0, 0, 0, 0), and the keyword fillcolor='red' gave (255, 0, 0). The Pillow page of rotate() names a fill colour and no operating system. Windows and macOS were never used, so that part of the chapter's sentence is read and not run. With expand=True the picture grows to hold the turned one: 120 by 80 becomes 142 by 118 at 20 degrees, and on the book's 816 by 1088 cat 6 degrees gives 926 by 1168; rotate(90) without expand keeps 120 by 80 and cuts the corners, with expand it is 80 by 120. transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT) mirrors the picture, so the left pixel is the old right pixel, and the old constant Image.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT also still works. resize() takes integers: floats raise TypeError with the text 'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer, which is why the chapter wraps the division in int(); and with no filter named it uses bicubic for an RGB picture. putpixel() returns None and takes a tuple, not a colour name; getpixel((-1, 0)) is the pixel of the last column. The sheet on the right is the picture the program saved: six panels on a beige ground, so the transparent corners of the RGBA copy show the ground and the others do not. The corpus program rotateFlipPixels_v1_0_0.py ran the same checks on a 60 by 40 gradient.
slides.take: The fill of a rotated corner follows the mode of the picture.

slides.notes: save() chooses the format from the extension. The cat, zophie.png, is 1,287,443 bytes as a PNG; saved as a JPEG at quality 95, 75, 50, 30 and 10 it is 327,361, 125,433, 81,267, 58,200 and 29,630 bytes, which the chart shows in kilobytes; the deck check computes the six numbers again every time it runs. JPEG is lossy: reading the quality 75 file back changes the largest channel value by 37, and the picture on the lower right shows the face as a PNG and as a JPEG of quality 10, side by side. A mode with an alpha channel cannot be written as JPEG, which raises OSError with cannot write mode RGBA as JPEG, and an extension Pillow does not know raises ValueError. The chapter says that Pillow's PNG files are 72 pixels per inch by default, and the program shows that they are not: a PNG saved with no dpi has no pHYs chunk and no density to read back, dpi is None; with dpi=(72, 72) the chunk holds 2835 pixels per metre, which Pillow reads as 72.009 dpi; a JPEG saved with the defaults has the density (1, 1) and unit 0, no unit at all; and a PNG that Matplotlib saves carries 100 dpi, as the graph slides show. The sums of the seating cards are right, 4 by 5 inches at 72 pixels per inch is 288 by 360 pixels, but that is arithmetic and not a property of the file. Wikipedia's article on PNG says the motivation for creating the format was the announcement on 28 December 1994 that implementations of GIF would have to pay royalties to Unisys for their patent of the LZW compression algorithm. Thomas Boutell posted a thread on comp.graphics on 4 January 1995 in which he devised a plan for a free alternative. The article gives the initial release of PNG as 1 October 1996. In this study img.save(buffer, 'PNG') and a reopen gave back the format PNG, and the format keeps the alpha channel that chapter 21 uses for its logo. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'PNG' (announcement on 28 December 1994; Boutell's posting on 4 January 1995; initial release 1 October 1996), read 2026-10-13; this study's leaves SaveFormats and PasteMask. The story of JPEG, which the notes carry and the slide does not: Wikipedia's article on JPEG says the Joint Photographic Experts Group created the standard in 1992 and that its lossy compression is based on the discrete cosine transform. That transform was first proposed by Nasir Ahmed as an image compression technique in 1972. The article gives the initial release as 18 September 1992. In this study img.save(buffer, 'JPEG') and a reopen gave back the format JPEG, the format chapter 21 uses for the photographs of its logo project. items.head: Resize only big ones
items.body: Both sides must be larger than 300. A strip of 1200 by 250 keeps its size, a panorama of 1200 by 400 becomes 300 by 100.

slides.notes: The flow chart is the book's Project 16, Adding a Logo to Every Picture. It opens catlogo.png once, then loops over the names that os.listdir() returns, skips every name that does not end in .png or .jpg and the logo itself, opens the picture and reads its size, and resizes it only if both the width and the height are larger than 300, so that the longer side becomes 300. It pastes the logo in the lower-right corner with the logo as its own mask and saves the result in the folder withLogo, then goes back to the loop. The research ran the shipped file resizeAndAddLogo.py of the online materials, after its SHA-256 was checked, in a folder with four test pictures: a panorama of 1200 by 400, a strip of 1200 by 250, a tall.jpg and the cat zophie.png of 816 by 1088. The exit code was 0 and withLogo held four pictures: panorama.png of 300 by 100, strip.png of 1200 by 250, tall.jpg of 214 by 300 and zophie.png of 225 by 300. The strip kept its size because only one of its sides is larger than 300, and the cat shrank from 816 by 1088 to 225 by 300; the logo landed at (125, 205), the lower-right corner of the 225 by 300 picture, and the pixel there changed. The picture on the right is that cat with the logo, saved by the program of the next slide, and the build compares it with what the program saves now. The size is int(300 / 1088 * 816), which is 225; without int() the division gives 225.00000000000003, and resize() refuses a float. A file called UPPER.PNG was skipped, because the test endswith('.png') is case sensitive.

slides.notes: These six branches are the route of the deck. Image fundamentals: a colour is four integers from 0 to 255, the origin is the top left pixel, and a box excludes its right and bottom edge. Image editing: paste() changes the image in place, resize() takes integers only, and rotate() fills the corners by the mode of the picture. The logo project: resize only if both sides are larger than 300, paste the logo with the logo as the mask, and remember that the page has an en dash where the file has a minus sign. Drawing and the clipboard: a rectangle includes its last pixel, textbbox() replaced textsize(), and copy() needs xclip and a display. Matplotlib graphs: Agg returns from show() at once, pie() returns a PieContainer in 3.11, and savefig() comes before show(). The book and practice: Green of Table 21-1 is lime, matplotlib==3.92 is not a release, and the second edition used textsize. Together they answer the first question of the chapter, what a program can be shown to do with a picture on a machine with no screen and what can only be shown to fail, and the slides that say where a printed line differs answer the second. The map is drawn from the same specification as the interactive page.
slides.take: If a branch feels unproven, its slides hold the example.

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.sub: Every link was opened on the day this deck was made
slides.notes: Every link on this slide was opened on the day the deck was made, and the build records the status each answered. The textbook chapter is free to read online and holds every listing of the chapter; the online materials are the zip of 91 files that the programs of this deck download and check by SHA-256, and Appendix A is where the book pins Pillow 10.4.0 and the Matplotlib release it writes as 3.92. The reference links are the pages of Pillow and Matplotlib that the chapter relies on and the README of pyperclipimg. Four of the six stories of the chapter are on slides with their own link, on the slide itself: Russell Kirsch and the first scanned picture, alpha compositing, the Python Imaging Library and Matplotlib. The other two, on PNG and on JPEG, are told in the notes of the slide about saving, and their pages are the third group. The last group is the PNG specification of the W3C and the Pillow page on file formats. The rest of the sixty sources of the research, among them the release notes of Pillow, the API changes of Matplotlib, the PyPI metadata and the standards for JPEG and JFIF, are in the research package. No photograph of a person is used in the deck.
slides.take: Textbook, documentation, standards and history, all opened today.

slides.title: What you should now be able to say
slides.sub: Four claims, each carried by a result you saw printed

items: A box has its left and top, not its right and bottom; crop() and paste() copy first.
A rotated corner is filled by the mode; a PNG has no dpi unless you give one.
textbbox() measures text; the clipboard and a window need a display.
Appendix A pins a release that does not exist; pie() changed in 3.11.

slides.notes: Four claims, each carried by a result you saw printed. If you can say them in your own words and run the examples yourself, you have the chapter. The console rows of the grid, the box, the answer of Appendix B, the Agg window and the pins need Pillow, Matplotlib or packaging, so they run in a Python that has those; the first three need only Pillow, and the version rows need packaging. The rows were run again under Python 3.14.6 each time the deck was built, and the programs, and with them the sixteen pictures, were run again by the check that compares the slides with the recording. What was not run is marked on its slide: Windows and macOS, a real screen, Matplotlib 3.9.2 and 3.10.0 as wheels on Python 3.14.6, and the licence of the cat picture was not checked. Nothing was ever shown to a person on a screen by the clipboard program. The next chapter of the book automates the keyboard and the mouse, and what this chapter taught about checking what a program saves, and about reading a printed output with care, carries over.
slides.take: Questions are welcome; bring a picture problem to run.
